sections.title: Start here
sections.body:
Ethics questions ask what a licensed engineer must do when duties pull in different directions. The order never changes: the public first, then the client or employer, then other engineers.

The handbook prints the rules. You do not need to memorise them, but you need to know they are there and how they are organised.
pitfalls: Choosing the answer that protects the client or the engineer when the public is at risk.
Treating a seal as a formality: it means the work was done under your direct control.

tips.from: Mark Mattson, FE Ethics and Economics Session 2022
items: Read the Model Rules in the handbook before exam day so that you know what is there and where.
To sign and seal, you must be responsible for the design decisions and have reviewed the work in full. A general look-over is not enough.
If you did not check something, say so. Never state that a check was done when it was not.
Most questions yield to common sense plus the order of duties: public first.

bridge.plain: This topic asks what a professional engineer must do when duties pull in different directions, and how licences, contracts and liability work.
core: Public health, safety and welfare come first.
Work only within your competence, and seal only work done under your direct control.
Disclose conflicts of interest; refuse gifts that could sway your judgement.
A contract needs an offer, acceptance, something of value exchanged, and a lawful purpose.
bridge.links: It stands apart from the technical topics, but every design topic ends in someone sealing the work.
bridge.exam: Answer from the NCEES Model Rules printed in the handbook, not from one state's law or a firm's policy.

sections.title: Codes of ethics
sections.body:
A code of ethics sets out what a licensed engineer owes to the public, to employers and clients, and to other engineers. The NCEES Model Rules, printed in the handbook, are the version the exam uses.

The order of duties decides most questions. Public health, safety and welfare come first. Next comes faithful service to the employer or client: confidentiality, disclosing conflicts of interest, and taking payment from only one party unless everyone agrees. Last comes fairness to other engineers: honest claims about your own qualifications and no attempts to win work with gifts. When two answers both sound reasonable, pick the one that protects the public or brings a conflict into the open.
pitfalls: Choosing loyalty to the client over a real risk to the public.
Treating disclosure as optional: a conflict that is known and agreed to in writing is allowed, a hidden one is not.

ideas.title: Report what you see, within your competence
ideas.text: An engineer who notices a possible hazard outside the assignment should tell the client or employer. The duty is to report it, not to analyse something outside one's own field.

ideas.title: When told to do something improper
ideas.text: If instructed to do something wrong, such as charging hours to the wrong client, do the work correctly, object, and take it up the chain. If that fails, document it; resigning and reporting are the last steps. Complying, staying silent and going to the press are not the answer.

ideas.title: A test for grey areas
ideas.text: Ask whether you would be comfortable seeing the action reported publicly with your name on it. The exam applies the NCEES Model Rules, not the rules of any one state.

ideas.title: Order of obligations
ideas.text: The NCEES Model Rules set three duties in this order: to the public, to the employer or client, and to other licensees. The first and foremost responsibility is the health, safety and welfare of the public. When two duties pull in different directions, the public comes first.

ideas.title: When you are overruled
ideas.text: If your professional judgement is overruled and public safety is endangered, you must notify your employer or client and whatever other authority is appropriate. Staying quiet, or resigning without telling anyone, does not meet the duty.

ideas.title: Conflicts of interest
ideas.text: Disclose every known or potential conflict of interest to your employer or client. You may be paid by more than one party for the same project only if the circumstances are fully disclosed and all parties agree in writing.

ideas.title: Gifts and payments
ideas.text: Do not solicit or accept gratuities from contractors, their agents or other parties in connection with work for an employer or client, and do not give anything of value to secure work. The test is whether it could influence, or appear to influence, your judgement.

ideas.title: Competence and truthfulness
ideas.text: Take on only the work you are qualified for by education or experience. Professional statements must be objective and truthful, and a public opinion must rest on adequate knowledge of the facts.

ideas.title: How the exam asks this
ideas.text: Expect a short scenario with four possible actions. The right answer protects the public, discloses rather than conceals, and stays within the engineer's competence and authority. Doing nothing and quietly complying are almost never correct.

sections.deep:
Codes of ethics rank an engineer's duties so that conflicts have an answer. The NCEES Model Rules, printed in the handbook, are the version the exam uses. Read each scenario by asking whose interest is at stake: the public, the employer or client, or other licensees, in that order.

The rules are mostly about honesty and independence: tell the truth in reports and testimony, stay within your competence, disclose anything that could bias your judgement, keep client information confidential and never trade favours for work.
method: Identify who could be harmed and which duty applies.
Eliminate any option that hides information or leaves a safety hazard in place.
Prefer the option that discloses to the client or employer first and escalates to an authority if the hazard remains.
If two options both seem ethical, choose the one the Model Rules state explicitly.

sections.primer: A code of ethics is a written list of duties. For engineers the first duty is to the public's safety, then to clients and employers, then to the profession. Questions describe a situation and ask which action the rules require.

sections.title: Professional liability
sections.body:
Professional liability is legal responsibility for harm caused by your professional work. An engineer is not expected to be perfect. The test is the standard of care: what a reasonably careful engineer would have done in the same situation.

To succeed in a negligence claim, the injured party must show a duty, a breach of that duty, harm, and that the breach caused the harm. Engineers manage this risk with careful practice, clear contracts, good records and professional liability (errors and omissions) insurance. Other policies cover other things: general liability for injury or property damage, workers' compensation for employees, builder's risk for the work in progress.
pitfalls: Assuming any defect means negligence. The question is whether the standard of care was met.
Confusing professional liability insurance with general liability insurance.

ideas.title: Say what you did not check
ideas.text: A partial review that others take for a complete one is how failures get through. State plainly the limits of what you reviewed.

ideas.title: Negligence
ideas.text: A negligence claim needs four elements: a duty owed, a breach of that duty, causation and actual damages. All four must be shown.

ideas.title: Standard of care
ideas.text: An engineer is judged against the care and skill ordinarily used by reasonably prudent engineers doing similar work in similar circumstances. The standard is competence, not perfection, so a bad outcome alone does not prove negligence.

ideas.title: Kinds of liability
ideas.text: Liability can arise in tort (negligence), in contract (failing to do what was agreed) or, for product makers, as strict liability, where fault need not be proved.

ideas.title: Insurance
ideas.text: Professional liability insurance, also called errors and omissions, covers claims that design errors caused loss. General liability covers bodily injury and property damage from operations. Workers' compensation covers a firm's own employees.

ideas.title: Time limits
ideas.text: A statute of limitations starts when the damage is discovered. A statute of repose starts at a fixed event such as substantial completion and sets an outer limit however late the defect appears.

ideas.title: Reducing exposure
ideas.text: Use a written scope, keep records of decisions, have work checked, stay within your competence and state clearly what was and was not relied upon.

sections.deep:
Professional liability is the legal side of ethics. An engineer who agrees to do work owes a duty of care to the client and to anyone who could foreseeably be harmed. Falling below the standard of care, and so causing damage, is negligence.

Contracts allocate that risk. Indemnification clauses shift it, limitation-of-liability clauses cap it and insurance pays for it. Good practice reduces it: a clear scope, documented decisions, checking and staying within one's competence.
method: Check the four elements of negligence: duty, breach, causation, damages.
Compare the conduct with what a reasonably prudent engineer would have done, not with a perfect result.
Match the type of loss to the policy that covers it.
Separate contract claims (what was promised) from tort claims (the duty of care).
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: Liability means being legally answerable for harm. An engineer is expected to work as carefully as a competent peer would. Falling short of that is negligence. Insurance and contract terms decide who pays.

sections.title: Licensure
sections.body:
A license is the state's permission to offer engineering services to the public. The usual path is an accredited degree, the FE exam, about four years of qualifying experience and the PE exam. Each state licenses separately. An engineer licensed in one state can apply to another by comity.

A seal on a document means the engineer was in responsible charge: direct control and personal supervision of the work. Engineers may seal only work in their area of competence that was prepared under their responsible charge. Boards can discipline licensees for misconduct, incompetence or fraud.
pitfalls: Sealing work you only reviewed briefly, or work outside your competence.
Assuming a license from one state allows practice in another.

ideas.title: What may be sealed
ideas.text: You may seal your own work, work by staff that you directed and reviewed in detail, and the coordination of a whole project when each discipline seals its own part. A general look over someone else's design is not responsible charge.

ideas.title: Grounds for discipline
ideas.text: Boards act on fraud, gross negligence, incompetence, misconduct and impairment such as habitual intoxication. Personal financial trouble, or giving an honest opinion founded on the facts, are not grounds.

ideas.title: What a licence means
ideas.text: A licence certifies minimum competence to practise, not expertise in every field. Model experience requirements shorten with graduate degrees.

ideas.title: The path to a license
ideas.text: The usual route is an accredited engineering degree, the FE exam, about four years of progressive experience under a licensed engineer, then the PE exam. Each state or territory board sets its own requirements. Passing the FE leads to engineer intern status.

ideas.title: One jurisdiction at a time
ideas.text: A license is valid only where it was issued. To practise or offer services in another state you need that state's license, normally obtained through comity, where the second board accepts your existing credentials instead of re-examining you.

ideas.title: Responsible charge and the seal
ideas.text: Sign and seal only documents prepared under your responsible charge, meaning your direct control and personal supervision, and only in areas where you are competent. Sealing work you did not supervise is a violation even if the work is correct.

ideas.title: Discipline
ideas.text: Boards can reprimand, fine, suspend or revoke a license for fraud, gross negligence, incompetence or misconduct. Licensees who know of a violation are expected to report it to the board and cooperate with it.

ideas.title: Keeping the license
ideas.text: Renewal usually requires continuing education, and a licensee must follow the laws and rules of every jurisdiction in which they practise.

sections.deep:
Licensure protects the public by restricting the practice of engineering to people who have shown competence. The Model Law in the handbook defines the terms: practice of engineering, responsible charge, engineer intern and the board's powers.

Each jurisdiction issues its own licence, so the questions usually turn on three ideas: you need a licence where the project is, you seal only what you supervised and are competent in, and the board can discipline violations including practising without a licence.
method: Find where the work is located; that jurisdiction's law applies.
Ask whether the engineer had responsible charge of the work being sealed.
Ask whether the work is within the engineer's area of competence.
When in doubt, choose the option that involves the licensing board or obtaining the proper licence.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: A licence is the state's permission to practise engineering. It is earned by education, exams (the FE, then the PE) and experience, and it is kept by renewal. A seal on a drawing means a licensed engineer takes responsibility for it.

sections.title: Contracts and contract law
sections.body:
A contract is an agreement the law will enforce. It needs an offer, an acceptance, consideration (each side gives something of value), parties able to contract and a lawful purpose.

Construction contracts differ in who carries the cost risk. In a lump sum contract the contractor does. In a unit price contract the owner pays for measured quantities. In cost plus contracts the owner pays actual cost and a fee. A breach is a failure to do what was promised; the usual remedy is money damages that put the other party where it would have been. Changes to the work are made by written change order.
pitfalls: Thinking a contract must be written to be valid. Many oral contracts are enforceable, though hard to prove.
Mixing up lump sum (fixed total) with unit price (fixed rate per quantity).

ideas.title: What makes a contract
ideas.text: An enforceable contract needs an offer, acceptance, consideration (something of value exchanged), competent parties and a lawful purpose. A missing element makes the agreement void or voidable.

ideas.title: Payment types and who carries the risk
ideas.text: Lump sum or fixed price: the contractor carries the cost risk. Unit price: payment follows measured quantities, so the owner carries quantity risk. Cost plus a fee: the owner carries the cost risk. A guaranteed maximum price caps the owner's exposure.

ideas.title: Breach and remedies
ideas.text: A material breach excuses the other party from performing and allows a claim for damages. Compensatory damages put the injured party where performance would have. Liquidated damages are a sum agreed in advance, typically per day of late completion.

ideas.title: Changes
ideas.text: A change order is a written amendment to scope, price or time, signed by the parties after award. Work done on an oral instruction is a common source of disputes.

ideas.title: Privity and agency
ideas.text: Only the parties to a contract can enforce it; that relationship is privity. An engineer administering a construction contract usually acts as the owner's agent and has no contract with the contractor.

sections.deep:
A contract is a set of promises the law will enforce. Engineering questions focus on formation (was there a valid contract?), performance (who has to do what, and who carries which risk?) and breach (what happens when a party does not perform?).

Read the payment terms to see who carries cost risk, and the documents to see what was actually promised. Changes after signing need a written change order. Only parties to a contract can enforce it, which is why a contractor's claim normally runs to the owner and not to the owner's engineer.
method: Check the elements: offer, acceptance, consideration, competent parties, lawful purpose.
Identify the contract type from how payment is set.
Decide who carries the risk that actually occurred.
For a dispute, ask what the written documents say and whether a change order exists.
sections.primer: A contract is an agreement the law will enforce. It needs an offer, an acceptance, something of value given by each side, parties able to agree, and a lawful purpose. Construction contracts differ mainly in who carries the risk of cost.
